name: Thymopentin

lead: Thymopentin is a five-amino-acid peptide (arginine, lysine, aspartate, valine, tyrosine) based on the thymus hormone thymopoietin and classed as an immunostimulant. Interest for looks comes from its use in skin conditions: calmer skin when inflammatory disease is involved.

The chain runs from a thymus-derived peptide to changes in T-cell activity to calmer skin in inflammatory disease. It has been tested in HIV, atopic dermatitis, cancer and other immune-related conditions. No published trial has tested it for an appearance outcome.

paras: It is used in some countries as an immune drug; in peptide circles it is mentioned as an immune-modulating compound. Much recent work concerns delivery systems because peptides are poorly absorbed orally.
Safety information was not covered in the sources reviewed. Its regulatory status varies by country, and it is not an approved appearance treatment.

angle.text: Thymopentin is an immune peptide used in some countries for infections and studied in skin conditions such as atopic dermatitis and eczema, where the hoped-for payoff is calmer skin. Trials on cosmetic outcomes have not been reported.

lead: Thymopentin (also abbreviated TP5 or TP-5) is a synthetic pentapeptide made of the amino acids arginine, lysine, aspartate, valine and tyrosine, corresponding to residues 32 to 36 of thymopoietin, a 49-amino-acid hormone secreted by epithelial cells of the thymus. It is classed as an immunostimulant (ATC code L03AX09) and is described as interacting with T cells.[1][2]

Its place in appearance and longevity discussion is through the thymus and immune ageing: researchers have described thymopentin as immunonormalizing in animal models of immune imbalance, including the thymic involution associated with ageing, and people interested in healthy-ageing peptides sometimes list it with other thymic peptides.[2] The one study in a skin condition is a 1990 double-blind trial in atopic dermatitis, where thymopentin was associated with greater reductions in severity, itching and redness than placebo.[3]

Published human research otherwise concentrates on immune-related conditions, including early AIDS-era studies, rheumatoid arthritis and cancer, and no trial of it for an appearance outcome such as wrinkles or physique has been found.[1][4]

paras: The thymus is a primary lymphoid organ in which immature T cells mature, with signalling molecules including thymulin, thymopoietin and the thymosins supporting that process.[5] It is most active in fetal and early life, reaches its relative maximum size around puberty at roughly 20 to 50 g, and then involutes, with fat and connective tissue gradually replacing thymic tissue until the gland may weigh only 5 to 15 g in old age, although some T-cell development continues in adults.[5]

This age-related shrinkage is the reason thymic peptides come up in healthy-ageing discussions. Thymopentin is a five-amino-acid fragment of thymopoietin, and its proponents and researchers describe it as mimicking the hormone's active site in immune regulation.[2] Wikipedia's thymopentin article lists its medical-literature uses as immune-related conditions, including early AIDS-era studies, rheumatoid arthritis and cancer, rather than cosmetic outcomes.[1]

A 1985 review reports that thymopentin appears to represent the active site of thymopoietin, with all the biological activities of the native hormone, which affects neuromuscular transmission, early T-cell differentiation and immune regulation. According to the review, its actions on peripheral T cells involve rises in intracellular cyclic GMP, in contrast to the cyclic AMP rises induced in precursor T cells that trigger their differentiation.[2]

In animal models the review describes thymopoietin and thymopentin as immunonormalizing, with effects seen whether the imbalance was toward hyper- or hyporesponsiveness, including imbalance induced by thymectomy or the thymic involution of ageing; the authors suggested potential utility in human diseases characterised by immune imbalance.[2] The only mechanistic detail in Wikipedia's entry is a 2007 study of thymopentin binding to HLA-DR molecules.[1]

Because peptides are poorly absorbed when swallowed, a body of pharmaceutics research has examined carriers for delivering thymopentin, including lectin-conjugated PLGA nanoparticles for oral delivery and inhalable microparticles loaded with solid lipid nanoparticles for the lungs.[6][7][8]

A two-centre, double-blind trial randomised 100 patients with moderate to severe atopic dermatitis to daily subcutaneous injections of thymopentin (Timunox, 48 patients) or placebo (52 patients) for six weeks. Both groups showed progressive declines in severity, but the reduction in the clinical severity score was larger with thymopentin (p = 0.04), with significant differences in itching (p = 0.02) and redness (p = 0.04), and no serious adverse experiences were seen in either group. The authors concluded that thymopentin was safe and offered therapeutic promise.[3][3] A 1989 review addressed thymopentin in dermatology more broadly.[9]

Wikipedia reports that early AIDS-era studies, from about 1983 to 1985, tested thymopentin, and that it helped to improve immunological condition in some patients for a brief time.[1] ClinicalTrials.gov lists a number of registered HIV-related studies of thymopentin, sold as Timunox in some registrations, including a double-blind study in asymptomatic infected patients on antiretroviral therapy and a phase 2 study of 60 patients receiving other anti-HIV drugs.[10][11]

Wikipedia notes use of thymopentin in rheumatoid arthritis in a 1994 report, and a review in Arzneimittel-Forschung covered thymopentin treatment of the condition.[1][12] A 2011 Cochrane review of thymic peptides in cancer identified 26 randomised trials with 2,736 patients, of which six tested synthetic thymic peptides (thymopentin or thymosin alpha 1). The reviewers found no benefit on overall survival for purified thymus extracts, found good tolerability and noted that most trials had at least a moderate risk of bias.[4] A phase 3 trial in patients after resection of small hepatocellular carcinoma has its status recorded as unknown.[13][13]
More recent investigations cover lung cancer, sepsis and infection prophylaxis in peritoneal dialysis, per Wikipedia.[1]
No studies of thymopentin for skin ageing, wrinkles, hair or physique were found.

Thymopoietin was identified as a thymus hormone, and the pentapeptide TP5 was characterised as its active fragment, in the research summarised by the 1985 review.[2] Early clinical testing took place in the AIDS epidemic: Wikipedia cites 1983 and 1984 reports of stimulated cellular function and preliminary clinical results in AIDS patients, and a 1985 report in AIDS and pre-AIDS patients.[1] Wikipedia lists no brand names or legal status for it; trial registrations use the name Timunox.[1][10]

timeline.event: First reports of thymopentin treatment in AIDS patients.[1]
Review describes thymopentin as the active site of thymopoietin.[2]
